subject: Biology
title: What Is DNA?
description: A quick win: understand What Is DNA?.

hook.text: Inside nearly every cell in your body sits a molecule that contains the blueprint for you.

buildup.text: DNA stands for deoxyribonucleic acid. It's a long chain of chemical letters: A, T, C, and G.

discovery.text: These four letters spell out instructions for building every protein your body needs.

twist.text: Stretched out, the DNA in one cell would reach about two meters long—yet it fits in a nucleus.

climax.text: Every living organism on Earth uses the same four-letter code. Life shares one language.

punchline.text: Four letters write the book of life.

quiz.question: What are the four chemical letters of DNA?

details.summary: DNA, deoxyribonucleic acid, is the molecule that stores and transmits genetic information in nearly all living organisms. Its four-letter code of adenine, thymine, guanine, and cytosine encodes the instructions for building every protein an organism needs.
details.whyItMatters: DNA is the blueprint of life. Understanding its structure and function is the foundation of genetics, medical research, forensics, evolutionary biology, and biotechnology, touching nearly every field of modern science.
takeaways: DNA uses four nucleotide bases: A, T, G, and C to store information
The sequence of bases encodes instructions for building proteins
DNA replicates itself before cell division to pass genes to daughter cells

faq.question: How much DNA is in a single human cell?
faq.answer: Each cell contains about 2 meters of DNA packed into a nucleus 6 micrometers wide. The total DNA from all cells in your body, if uncoiled and laid end to end, would stretch to the sun and back hundreds of times.

faq.question: Why is DNA so stable compared to other biological molecules?
faq.answer: The double helix structure protects the bases inside like rungs of a ladder. The sugar-phosphate backbone resists chemical degradation. DNA repair enzymes constantly scan for and fix damage. This stability allows DNA to preserve information across billions of years.
